headline: Wall Street closes at fresh records on Hormuz de-escalation hopes while KSE-100 slips 0.63% on profit-taking and oil tumbles over 5%
mood: Cautiously constructive · oil and the Fed are the swing factors

five_things.html: The S&P 500 (+1.79%), Dow (+1.71%, above 54,000 for the first time) and Nasdaq (+2.59%) all closed at records on Tuesday as easing US-Iran tensions over the Strait of Hormuz and a tech rebound drove the strongest rally in months (CNN, CNBC).

The KSE-100 fell 0.63% to 177,083.22 (−1,116.80 pts), giving back part of Monday's 1.20% surge as breadth turned negative — 161 advancers vs 295 decliners on 711.3m shares (Rs25.9bn) (Express Tribune, Trading Economics).
Brent (−5.3% to $79.36) and WTI (−5.7% to $75.77) tumbled as diplomacy hopes eased Strait of Hormuz supply risk, even as OPEC+ layered on 188,000 bpd of extra August supply (Rigzone, Saudi Gazette).
Gold held near $4,075 and silver near $58.63 as Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish-tinted 29 July hold left markets pricing roughly a 65% chance of a September hike rather than a cut (CNBC).

CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July from 11.1% in June, giving the SBP room to hold its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting, while Gulf non-oil PMIs (Saudi 53.1, UAE 55.8) stayed comfortably expansionary (Business Recorder, AGBI).

matrix.local_html: Tuesday's session saw the KSE-100 retreat 0.63% to 177,083.22, shedding 1,116.80 points as institutional profit-taking followed Monday's 1.20% surge to 178,200.02. Breadth turned negative — 295 decliners against 161 advancers on 711.3 million shares (Rs25.9bn) — with Trading Economics confirming the pullback. Meezan Bank, PSO, Kapco, Power Cement and Millat Tractors added a combined 175 points, but UBL, Engro Holdings, OGDC, Lucky Cement and PPL erased 580 points on selective profit-taking in banks and E&P names. On the macro front, headline CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July from 11.1% in June, giving the SBP room to hold its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting. Six-month KIBOR is tracking near 11.70–11.90% (EST.). The IMF's Executive Board cleared the third EFF/RSF review in May, unlocking roughly $1.2bn; the next mission, likely covering an Article IV consultation, is expected in H2 2026.
matrix.gcc_html: Gulf oil producers added to August supply as seven OPEC+ members agreed to raise output by 188,000 bpd, split across Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman, continuing the unwind of 2023's voluntary cuts. That extra supply landed just as Brent slid 5.3% to a three-week low of $79.36 on hopes for a reopened Strait of Hormuz — a double-barrelled bearish setup for crude that nonetheless keeps the Gulf's non-oil diversification story intact. Saudi Arabia's non-oil PMI held at a still-robust 53.1 in July (53.3 in June), while the UAE's PMI eased to 55.8 from 57.1 — its slowest pace in three months, though new export orders hit a three-year high as demand broadened across the GCC and Europe, a supportive signal for Vision 2030-linked non-oil diversification.
matrix.global_html: Wall Street closed at fresh records on Tuesday — the S&P 500 jumped 1.79% to 7,736.52, the Dow added 907 points (+1.71%) to close above 54,000 for the first time, and the Nasdaq surged 2.59% to 26,584.99, powered by a tech rebound, strong earnings, and easing US-Iran tensions over Hormuz. Bonds told a more cautious story: the 10-year yield sits near 4.63% and the 2-year at 4.21%, with markets pricing roughly a 65% chance the Fed hikes rather than cuts in September after Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish-sounding hold on 29 July rattled the inflation-credibility narrative. Separately, Washington's trade agenda intensified: a 50% ad valorem tariff on Canadian goods takes effect 19 August, alongside Section 301 forced-labor duties of 10–12.5% on roughly 60 economies that took effect 24 July.

legislative.policy_html: Finance Act 2026 rolls out a 5% withholding tax on social media revenue and a National Faceless Center for algorithm-based tax audits/appeals, effective 1 July 2026.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: FBR digitisation vendors, compliant formal-sector filers. Loses: social-media creators/platforms, cash-heavy informal retailers facing a tighter net.

legislative.policy_html: Saudi Arabia's new Companies Law mandates beneficial-ownership disclosure and a unified commercial register; the UAE's Cabinet Decision No. 59 of 2026 competition-law regulations took effect 30 July.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: institutional investors and dealmakers gaining transparency, multinationals already compliant. Loses: opaque shell structures, SMEs absorbing new compliance overhead.

legislative.policy_html: Washington's 50% tariff on Canadian goods (cement, furniture, textiles) takes effect 19 August; Section 301 forced-labor tariffs of 10–12.5% on roughly 60 economies are already live since 24 July.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: US domestic manufacturers in tariffed categories. Loses: Canadian exporters, US importers/retailers and consumers facing higher input costs.

desk_stance_html: Desk view: Tuesday's pullback reads as profit-taking after a sharp two-session advance, not a trend reversal — breadth stayed negative (161 advancers vs 295 decliners) but large-cap banks and energy names absorbed most of the selling. Global tailwinds hold: a sharp Brent/WTI drawdown on Hormuz de-escalation hopes is disinflationary for Pakistan's import bill, and Wall Street's record run keeps risk appetite supportive for EM flows. Watch 176,000 as the first floor; a close below opens 174,500. On the upside, reclaiming 178,200 re-opens Monday's high near 179,500. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.

🌅 Economic Vibes — Morning Brief | Wednesday, 05 August 2026

Wall Street closed at records overnight while the KSE-100 took a breather — here's what the desk is watching this morning.

THE OVERNIGHT TAPE
S&P 500 +1.79% to 7,736.52, Dow +1.71% to 54,085.88 (first close above 54,000), Nasdaq +2.59% to 26,584.99 — all-time highs driven by easing US-Iran tensions over the Strait of Hormuz and a tech rebound. US 10Y sits at 4.63%, 2Y at 4.21%, with markets now pricing ~65% odds of a Fed hike (not a cut) in September after Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish-leaning hold on 29 July.

PAKISTAN
KSE-100 slipped 0.63% to 177,083.22 (−1,116.80 pts), giving back part of Monday's 1.20% rally as breadth turned negative (161 advancers vs 295 decliners, 711.3m shares, Rs25.9bn). Banks and E&P names led the retreat (UBL, OGDC, PPL, Lucky Cement), while Meezan Bank, PSO and Power Cement held up. On the macro side: CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July from 11.1%, and the SBP held its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting. The IMF's Executive Board cleared the third EFF/RSF review in May, unlocking roughly $1.2bn; the next mission is expected in H2 2026.

GCC
OPEC+ added 188,000 bpd of August supply even as Brent (−5.3% to $79.36) and WTI (−5.7% to $75.77) tumbled on Hormuz de-escalation hopes. Saudi's non-oil PMI held at 53.1 in July; UAE's eased to 55.8 (slowest in three months) but export orders hit a three-year high — a supportive read for Vision 2030 diversification.

GLOBAL
Gold is holding near $4,075, silver near $58.63, as Fed policy uncertainty keeps havens bid even with equities at records. Washington's trade agenda is heating up: a 50% tariff on Canadian goods lands 19 August, and Section 301 forced-labor tariffs (10–12.5% on ~60 economies) are already in force since 24 July.

LEGISLATIVE TRACKER
Pakistan's Finance Act 2026 brings a 5% withholding tax on social media revenue and a faceless tax-audit system — wins for compliance-tech vendors, costs for creators and informal retailers.
Saudi's new Companies Law and the UAE's Cabinet Decision 59/2026 competition rules tighten disclosure — wins for institutional investors, added overhead for SMEs.
US tariffs on Canada (50%) and forced-labor goods (10–12.5%, ~60 economies) raise input costs for importers and retailers even as they shield targeted US manufacturers.

THE DAY AHEAD
KSE-100: support 176,000 (deeper at 174,500), pivot 177,083 (Tuesday's close), resistance 178,200 (Monday's close/high, then 179,500).
Desk view: Tuesday's dip reads as profit-taking, not reversal — falling oil is a tailwind for Pakistan's import bill, and global risk appetite stays supportive. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.
